Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette:
Margaret Weiss is an 80-year-old retired-not-retired social worker who still works part time with older adults at a community agency, and she describes her life as divided into a before and after that she never expected at her age. The trauma she speaks about happened in the context of a late-life romantic relationship that had seemed, at first, companionable and safe. She had known loneliness and was not naïve about disappointment, but she had still believed that by this stage of life people were more settled, more decent, less dangerous. The assault that now anchors her fear took place in his home after an argument escalated behind a closed door. What remains with her is not a smooth story but a set of fixed images: his face changing, the sudden movement of his body blocking her way, the door slamming, his hand on her, the angle of the room as she tried to orient herself, the sound of another door opening somewhere in the house. When she tries to tell it, the sequence breaks apart. She can offer only separate pictures, and when she reaches them she is overcome not only by fear but by a grief that feels larger than the incident itself, grief for the person she had been and for the ordinary faith in people she feels was taken from her.

In the weeks that followed, Margaret found herself thinking again and again about why this had happened to her. She could not stop returning to the question, as if some explanation might make the event fit into a moral world she recognized. Instead, the world itself began to feel altered. She had come to believe that her understanding of how people behave, of what intimacy means, of what safety in familiar company should look like, had been completely destroyed. Most painful to her was the conviction that people simply cannot be trusted. This did not stay confined to thoughts about her former partner. It spread outward, especially toward men, and even toward men she knew. If a male maintenance worker arrived at her apartment building unexpectedly, or if a male colleague lingered after a meeting until the room had emptied, she felt her body brace before she had time to think. Being alone with men became intolerable in a way she could not dismiss as irrational, because to her it felt proven. Even related people could set this off; a visit from a nephew or a family friend did not automatically register as safe simply because they were known.

Doors became especially potent. The sound of a door opening behind her at work, or a heavy office door slamming down the hall, could pull her up short and leave her heart racing. In the agency building where she meets clients, she now notices every entrance the moment she walks in. Before she sits down in a waiting room or an interview office, she scans for exits, checks where she would go, and keeps herself positioned so she is not trapped. She describes herself as constantly on guard, watchful in grocery stores, elevators, hallways, and church basements, anywhere an unexpected male presence or the abrupt movement of a door might occur. Colleagues have noticed that she prefers to leave her office door slightly open and that she is quicker than before to relocate conversations into more public spaces.

At night the injury remains close. Margaret has trouble falling asleep and often wakes after only short stretches, already tense. She has begun structuring her evenings around not dreaming. She avoids certain times and situations that she believes make nightmares more likely: lingering alone in the dark living room, dozing in her armchair, letting her mind drift before bed. She keeps herself occupied instead, sometimes sorting papers from work or leaving the television on longer than she wants, because the quiet feels dangerous. Alongside this, she tries forcefully to erase the memory altogether. If one of the images intrudes, she tells herself to stop, to clear it out, to put it somewhere inaccessible. Yet when it returns, it does so as those same isolated pictures rather than a narrative she can place in order.

She also speaks, with visible shame, about feeling dirty because of what happened. She knows how stark that sounds, especially as a seasoned social worker who has spent decades helping other people name injustice accurately. Still, the feeling persists. It leaves her scrubbing her hands longer than necessary after work and changing clothes quickly after difficult days, not because she thinks this makes logical sense but because contamination is how the experience sits in her body.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was the recognition that her life had narrowed around these precautions. She still values her work and does not want to withdraw from it, but she has started turning down home visits if she believes a man may answer the door, and she worries this is changing the kind of social worker she can be. More quietly, she is frightened by how thoroughly mistrust has entered her relationships and by the possibility that the world will never feel recognizable again. What she hopes for is modest but urgent: to sleep, to enter a room without immediately plotting escape, and to be able to remember what happened without being shattered by grief.
